A monitoring agent (TypeSafe Jev) read the routers and judged each log line on its own. These lines were judged FAILED:

  r1    r1 10.90.10.12 did not respond to SSH: ssh: connect to host 10.90.10.12 port 22: Connection timed out

Routers judged faulty: r1

Jev then chose which path should carry the traffic:
  PATH-B  (STANDBY, through r3 on the shared standby segment)


  Two paths join the client edge rc1 to the server edge rc2. They share no
  intermediate router.

     PATH-A   PRIMARY                     PATH-B   STANDBY

     rc1 ──pa──► r1                       rc1 ──st──► r3
           ──pb──► r2                            ──st──┐
                ──pc──► rc2  ◄──st───────────────────┘

     fwd next hop on rc1:  10.90.10.12        fwd next hop on rc1:  10.90.20.12
     rev next hop on rc2:  10.90.12.15        rev next hop on rc2:  10.90.20.12


Which path is already decided. Your job is HOW to make the routers actually carry traffic over it, safely, without stranding the return path.

How to be fast and correct:
  * Issue independent read-only commands together in one turn,     not one per turn.
  * Do not explore the topology. It is given above.
  * Read the routing table on rc1 and rc2 before changing     anything.
  * A non-zero exit on a command means the syntax was     rejected. That is a syntax error, not a network fault. Fix     the command; do not change strategy.
  * After every change, read the table back and confirm the     target path is now the active one.

What is wrong, and how can you fix it?
I'll start by reading the routing tables and checking whether r1 is genuinely down, all in one turn.

Done. Traffic is on PATH-B in both directions.

## What was wrong

The monitoring agent's diagnosis was correct: **r1 is really down**. I confirmed it independently — SSH gives `No route to host` from the agent side, and rc1's ping to 10.90.10.12 returns `Destination Host Unreachable`, which is ARP failing on the PA segment, not just an SSH service problem. r1 is unreachable at layer 2, so it will not come back on its own.

But the interesting failure was not r1 — it was what the routing tables were doing about it:

```
rc1: S>* 10.90.8.1/32 [1/0]   via 10.90.10.12   <-- PATH-A, ACTIVE, pointing at a dead box
     S   10.90.8.1/32 [200/0] via 10.90.20.12   <-- PATH-B, present but never selected
```

**PATH-B was already fully configured on both edges, and it was not carrying anything.** The AD-200 standby route can't be "promoted" by r1 dying, because static route preference is resolved by administrative distance alone — the kernel does not probe a next hop to see whether it answers before installing the lower-AD route. With AD 1 pointing at a black hole, the backup never gets installed, and the forward path is silently black-holed while everything still *looks* configured and healthy.

The second issue was the reverse direction. On rc2, `10.90.1.1/32` was still active via 10.90.12.15 — r2. r2 itself is fine and answers, but its route for the client is `via 10.90.11.13`, and 10.90.11.13 is r1's address on PB. So even with rc2 reachable, return traffic toward rc1 was pointed at dead r1. That's the "stranding the return path" case: a one-sided flip would have given a forward path over r3 with no way back.

## The fix

Verified PATH-B healthy *before* touching anything — r3 reachable from both rc1 and rc2, r3 answering on both of its ST addresses (10.90.20.11, 10.90.20.14), and r3 already holding routes to both end networks. Confirmed r2 is up and understood why its return path is dead.

Then withdrew both PATH-A routes in a single turn, so the two directions flipped together rather than leaving a window with one side still pointed at r1:

- `rc1: no ip route 10.90.8.1/32 10.90.10.12`
- `rc2: no ip route 10.90.1.1/32 10.90.12.15`

I withdrew rather than re-adding at a lower distance because r1's link-layer presence is gone — a floating route can't fail back to a next hop that doesn't ARP, so PATH-A should stay removed until r1 is actually repaired.

## Confirmed

Both edges now show a single route, `via 10.90.20.12`, and `ip route get` confirms the FIB agrees (via eth1, not the cached eth0 entry from before). Ping 10.90.8.1 from rc1 and 10.90.1.1 from rc2 both succeed at ~0.2ms, sub-millisecond as expected for two hops over the shared segment. Return path is intact, not stranded.

One thing worth flagging for follow-up: **r1 itself is still down and I did not fix that** — nothing here can, from the outside. The failover is complete, but PATH-A remains broken until someone restores r1's connectivity to the PA segment. Also note rc1 has other routes still using dead r1 as a next hop (`10.90.2.2/32` at AD 1 via 10.90.10.12), so any traffic to that destination is still black-holed on the same pattern; say the word and I'll clear those too.
